steps.observation: Work on this for 900 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The keeper’s name was Elias Finnegan, and for thirty-two years he had tended the glass-paned crown of Grayhaven Light. The tower rose from a black basalt headland like a single white candle, its wick a lantern whose beam swept the Atlantic in slow, patient arcs. In town they said no one knew the sea like Elias, yet few knew Elias himself; he came and went with the tides, solitary as the gull that coasted each morning on the updrafts.

On the night the story begins, November clouds pressed so low they seemed to scrape the lens room. The air tasted of brass and salt, and the wind carried a mournful note—something like an old fiddle heard through walls. Elias logged barometer readings, checked the oil pressure, and wound the timing mechanism until the lantern gears clicked into their familiar heartbeat. Routine calmed him; routine kept fear at bay.

But fear found cracks. Every autumn since his wife, Maren, had passed, he’d dreamed of her voice on stormy nights: “Mind the light, Eli. Ships follow hope, and hope follows the beam.” He could almost see her, shawl snapping in the gale, pointing seaward toward vessels invisible to mortal sight.

Thunder rolled like cannon fire, and the beacon’s beam wavered—briefly dimmed. Elias sprang up the iron staircase, boots ringing. In the lantern room he discovered the culprit: a loosened carburetor pin rattling inside the lamp housing. One careless second and half the coast would go dark. He removed his cap, pressed it into the crack to stifle the drafts, and worked by the jittery glow of a match until the mechanism was true again. The beacon pulsed strong, shaving pathways of white across the writhing water.

Far below, something answered: a single, distant horn. Through the curtain of rain Elias glimpsed a freighter pitching high, her navigation lights blinking SOS. She was off course, flirting with Wolfjaw Shoals, where granite teeth waited just beneath the waves. Elias gripped the railing hard enough to numb his fingers. He leaned into the wind and cranked the emergency sector shutters, tightening the light’s focus into a lance. Again he heard Maren: “Draw them home.”

Minutes dragged like hours while the sea battered stone. Then—silence. The horn ceased; the freighter’s bulk slid past the headland, missing the shoals by mere yards. Elias let out a breath he hadn’t realized he’d been holding, and the lantern glass fogged with relief.

When dawn finally bled pale pink across the horizon, a small launch approached the breakwater. Two deckhands climbed the ladder to bring news: their captain sent gratitude, a crate of oranges, and an invitation to dinner in port. Elias smiled, surprised how long it had been since someone had offered him ordinary company. He accepted. The deckhands turned to go, but one paused. “We kept wondering why your light blinked Morse for ‘home.’ Did you mean it for us?”

Elias glanced at the great lamp overhead, still turning, still faithful. Home, he thought, was a word bigger than houses or harbors. It was a promise, a beam that says keep going; the dark is not the end.

“I guess I did,” he said.

Later, alone again, he peeled an orange and watched the sunrise turn the sea to molten gold. The gull wheeled by, screaming delight at the wind. Elias Finnegan lifted a slice of fruit in silent toast—to Maren, to the freighter now beyond the curve of the world, and to the lighthouse that would keep shining long after even his steady hands were gone. Somewhere below, waves struck rock in never-ending applause, as if the ocean itself approved the bargain between hope and light.
